[17] assistant: Yes. I’d design this as **a masterclass in building and operating retrieval systems**, with vector storage as the foundation. Students should finish able to explain *why* a design works, measure its quality, and manage its failure modes.

I’ve saved a concrete [curriculum and implementation blueprint](/Users/markcastillo/git/vector-masterclass/docs/CURRICULUM.md) and a [project README](/Users/markcastillo/git/vector-masterclass/README.md). These are design documents; the notebooks and runtime have not been implemented yet.

Your chosen stack is a good fit:

- **Qdrant in local Docker Compose** for the actual database exercises.
- **Python and uv** for a reproducible environment.
- **CPU embeddings** with explicit model revisions and device selection.
- **Jupyter notebooks** for teaching, experiments, and visuals.
- A small shared Python package so notebooks, tests, and the eventual serving API use the same implementation.

**The curriculum should progress through six stages.**

| Stage | Coverage | What students demonstrate |
|---|---|---|
| Foundations | Vector geometry, similarity metrics, embeddings, tokenization, normalization, exact search, lexical search | Implement and explain a baseline without hiding the mechanics |
| Retrieval engineering | Qdrant data modeling, ingestion, chunking, metadata filters, HNSW, hybrid search, reranking | Improve retrieval quality against a fixed evaluation set |
| Applications | RAG, recommendations, deduplication, semantic caching, routing, agent memory, classification, multimodal search | Choose representations and metrics appropriate to each application |
| Advanced methods | Learned sparse retrieval, Matryoshka embeddings, late interaction, contextual retrieval, graph-assisted retrieval, visual document retrieval | Measure when added complexity helps |
| Production engineering | Serving, authorization, concurrency, freshness, migrations, observability, capacity, backups, replication | Operate the system and recover from failures |
| Capstone | An evaluated service with architectural decisions and operational exercises | Defend quality, latency, cost, and reliability tradeoffs with evidence |

The blueprint expands this into **30 proposed notebooks**, with a core path and optional application/research branches. I’d budget roughly **40–60 hours for the core**, plus additional time for advanced labs and the capstone, then revise those estimates after piloting.

**The most important additions to consider are these:**

1. **Teach evaluation before optimization.**  
   Introduce relevance judgments, Recall@k, MRR, and nDCG near the beginning. Distinguish “ANN found the same neighbors as exhaustive search” from “the retrieved documents answered the question.” Keep tuning queries separate from the final test set.

2. **Make ingestion and data lifecycle first-class topics.**  
   Include stable document/chunk IDs, provenance, retries, deduplication, updates, deletion, stale content, embedding versioning, and reindexing. Students should rebuild the index from retained source data and recover from an interrupted ingestion.

3. **Give non-RAG applications their own success criteria.**  
   Recommendation quality is different from retrieval relevance. Semantic caching needs false-hit tests. Entity matching needs false-merge analysis. Agent memory needs correction, expiration, and deletion behavior. These should be executable labs, not a list of potential use cases.

4. **Teach permissions as part of retrieval architecture.**  
   Tenant boundaries and document permissions must apply across candidate retrieval, reranking, caches, and returned evidence. Include negative tests where the system must return nothing, even when an unauthorized document is the closest semantic match.

5. **Include situations where vector search is the wrong choice.**  
   Compare against exact lookups, SQL predicates, lexical search, and simple exhaustive scans. Show identifier-heavy queries, small datasets, and transactional workloads where another approach may be simpler or more accurate.

6. **Make failures visible.**  
   Include negation, outdated instructions, contradictory documents, unanswerable questions, truncated inputs, poor chunk boundaries, revoked access, and malicious retrieved instructions. A useful exercise is: “The result looks plausible—find why it is wrong.”

7. **Separate retrieval quality from answer quality.**  
   RAG needs separate assessment of retrieved evidence, context assembly, answer correctness, citation support, and abstention. An LLM judge can assist, but should not be the only source of evaluation.

8. **Treat reproducibility as part of the lesson.**  
   Record dataset hashes, model revisions, settings, hardware, server/client versions, and warm/cold cache state. Every notebook should run from a fresh kernel and produce a readable static export.

For advanced coverage, I’d teach **established techniques plus a maintained research track**, rather than promise a permanently “most state-of-the-art” recipe. Qdrant’s documented multi-stage queries provide a practical basis for fusion and candidate rescoring. Matryoshka models and ColBERT-style late interaction introduce different quality/storage tradeoffs that students can investigate. [Qdrant multi-stage queries](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/hybrid-queries/), [Matryoshka research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13147), [ColBERTv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488).

The research track can extend to visual document retrieval and multi-vector compression. These should include small CPU experiments where feasible and explicitly labeled replay artifacts when the encoder is too expensive for a normal lesson. A small demonstration would teach the mechanism without claiming to reproduce the paper’s performance. [ColPali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449), [MUVERA](https://research.google/blog/muvera-making-multi-vector-retrieval-as-fast-as-single-vector-search/).

**Each notebook should follow a consistent teaching pattern:** an engineering question → intuition and necessary mathematics → a baseline → one controlled change → measured results and visuals → a failure case → an exercise → production implications. Useful visuals include ranking changes, similarity heatmaps, recall/latency curves, threshold precision/recall plots, and request traces. Two-dimensional embedding plots are useful illustrations, but should not stand in for retrieval evaluation.

Two practical decisions deserve explicit treatment:

- **CPU resource budgets.** Start with a small encoder, small reranker, and tiny/standard/scale dataset profiles. Measure batching, sequence length, threading, and optional ONNX inference. Keep model-weight quantization separate from stored-vector quantization. [Sentence Transformers CPU/backend guidance](https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/efficiency.html).
- **The generation backend.** CPU embeddings do not determine how answers are generated. I recommend a core course that requires no paid API, with retrieval and context assembly fully executable locally, plus an explicit real-generation extension. Extractive displays or prerecorded answers must be labeled as such.

For the production section, require **restore, migration, and failure exercises**, not just deployment instructions. A three-node Compose setup can teach replication behavior, while remaining a single-host experiment. Snapshot exercises must also account for external metadata and aliases; Qdrant collection snapshots do not include aliases, and distributed snapshots are node-scoped. [Qdrant snapshot documentation](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/operations/snapshots/).

The first implementation milestone should be a complete vertical slice: **uv + Jupyter + Compose Qdrant + CPU encoder + a small corpus + exact and lexical baselines + retrieval metrics + a few polished notebooks**. That will establish the teaching style and validate laptop feasibility before expanding to the full course.

[24] assistant: **The direction is good, but I’d tighten five parts before treating this as the implementation specification.** The stack and overall architecture fit the goal. The main risks are misleading experiments, an incomplete RAG experience, and too much material packed into individual notebooks.

I reviewed the full blueprint and checked Qdrant’s indexing behavior against its documentation.

1. **High priority: make relevance judgments independent of chunking.**  
   The design compares chunking strategies, but it does not define how relevance labels survive changes to chunk boundaries. If labels attach to the original chunks, changing chunk size changes the evaluation target. Overlapping chunks can also inflate apparent success.

   **Fix:** anchor gold evidence to source document revisions and source spans. Define how retrieved chunks map to that evidence, deduplicate document-level results, and compare context quality under a fixed token budget as well as fixed `k`. Explicitly define metric handling for unanswerable queries and partially judged datasets.  
   See [evaluation data design](/Users/markcastillo/git/vector-masterclass/docs/CURRICULUM.md:121).

2. **High priority: ensure the ANN lab actually exercises an ANN index.**  
   The small datasets are sensible for teaching, but Qdrant does not automatically index every segment; optimizer settings and segment size matter, and filter cardinality influences query planning. Without an explicit setup check, students could vary HNSW parameters while effectively measuring scans and draw incorrect conclusions. [Qdrant indexing documentation](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/indexing/)

   **Fix:** give the ANN notebook a dedicated configuration and dataset profile. Verify index construction has completed, record indexing and scan thresholds, account for filter selectivity, and separate ingestion/index-building time from query benchmarks. An inconclusive parameter sweep should be reported as inconclusive.  
   See [the ANN lesson](/Users/markcastillo/git/vector-masterclass/docs/CURRICULUM.md:48).

3. **Medium priority: resolve the generation dependency across the core course.**  
   Generation is optional in notebook 12, but notebook 13 includes query rewriting, decomposition, contextual retrieval, and iterative retrieval. Those require either a real model, supplied transformations, or explicitly simplified implementations. As written, the default path could finish without executing an actual generative RAG system.

   **Fix:** define two explicit execution profiles: retrieval-only and live RAG. Make one small end-to-end live RAG exercise required for completing the RAG track, with a selected backend, resource limits, citations, and no-answer tests. Prewritten rewrites can teach retrieval mechanics, but should not count as executing model-driven rewriting.
